title: AWS Compute: EC2, Storage, Load Balancing and Auto Scaling
intro: Amazon EC2 (Elastic Compute Cloud) is the AWS service that rents you virtual machines, called instances, by the second, and around it sit the services that make those machines useful: EBS disks, Elastic Load Balancing, and EC2 Auto Scaling. This lesson teaches how each piece works, how it is priced, and how they combine into a web tier that survives the loss of a data center and grows or shrinks with demand.

sections.heading: EC2 fundamentals: instances, AMIs and instance types
sections.content:
An **EC2 instance** is a virtual machine running on AWS hardware. You choose the operating system, the amount of CPU and memory, the disk, and the network placement, and AWS gives you a running server within about a minute. Think of renting a furnished office by the hour instead of buying a building: you pay for the time you use, and you hand it back when you are done.

### The AMI: the template for a machine

Every instance starts from an **Amazon Machine Image (AMI)**. An AMI bundles three things: a snapshot of a root volume (the operating system and any pre-installed software), launch permissions (who may use it), and a block device mapping (which disks to attach). AMIs come from four places: AWS itself (Amazon Linux, Windows Server), the AWS Marketplace (vendor-built images), the community, and your own account (a **golden image** you baked after configuring a server). An AMI is **regional**: an image in one Region must be copied before it can be used in another.

### Instance types and families

An instance type name encodes its purpose. Take **m6i.xlarge**: the letter m is the family, 6 is the generation, i means an Intel processor (g means AWS Graviton, a means AMD), and xlarge is the size. Within one family, each size step up roughly doubles vCPU and memory.

| Family | Optimized for | Example types | Typical workload |
|---|---|---|---|
| General purpose | Balanced CPU, memory, network | t3, t4g, m6i, m7g | Web servers, small databases, dev/test |
| Compute optimized | High CPU per dollar | c6i, c7g | Batch processing, encoding, game servers |
| Memory optimized | Large RAM | r6i, x2idn | In-memory caches, big databases, analytics |
| Storage optimized | Fast local disk, high IOPS | i4i, d3 | NoSQL stores, data warehouses |
| Accelerated computing | GPUs and custom chips | p4d, g5, inf2 | Machine learning, graphics rendering |

The **t family is burstable**: it earns CPU credits while idle and spends them under load. That is cheap for a lightly used server, but a t3 that runs hot all day exhausts its credits and slows down (or, in unlimited mode, costs extra). A frequent beginner mistake is putting a steady, busy workload on a burstable type.

### What matters and what to ask

The questions a practitioner asks before picking a type: Is the workload limited by CPU, memory, disk or network? Does it run steadily or in bursts? Does the software support Arm (Graviton), which is often cheaper for the same performance? **Right-sizing** means matching the type to measured usage, and tools such as CloudWatch metrics and AWS Compute Optimizer help you do it. Over-provisioning (choosing a big instance just in case) is the most common source of wasted spend, so start small and measure.

sections.heading: The instance lifecycle, user data and key pairs
sections.content:
An instance moves through well-defined states, and each state has a different billing consequence. Knowing them prevents both surprise bills and accidental data loss.

### Lifecycle states

| State | Meaning | Compute billing | Root EBS volume |
|---|---|---|---|
| pending | Starting up | Not yet billed | Being attached |
| running | Usable | Billed per second | Billed |
| stopping / stopped | Shut down but kept | Not billed | Still billed |
| shutting-down / terminated | Deleted forever | Not billed | Deleted by default |

The important distinctions:

- **Stop** is like powering off a PC. The instance keeps its EBS volumes and private IP, but it loses its automatically assigned public IPv4 address, and it may start later on different physical hardware. Only EBS-backed instances can be stopped.
- **Reboot** is a restart on the same host. Nothing changes: same IP, same disks, even instance store data survives.
- **Hibernate** saves RAM to the encrypted root volume so the instance resumes exactly where it left off.
- **Terminate** is permanent. The instance is gone, and the root volume is deleted unless its DeleteOnTermination flag was turned off. This is irreversible, so production instances often enable **termination protection**.

A classic pitfall: stopping an instance feels like it saves everything, yet you still pay for its EBS volumes and any idle Elastic IP address. Another: relying on an auto-assigned public IP that changes on every stop/start. If you need a fixed address, allocate an **Elastic IP**, or better, put a load balancer with a DNS name in front.

### User data: configuration at first boot

**User data** is a script (up to 16 KB) you supply at launch. On Linux AMIs it is executed by cloud-init as root, by default only on the first boot. It is how you turn a generic image into a configured server without logging in.

```bash
#!/bin/bash
dnf install -y nginx
echo Hello from $(hostname -f) > /usr/share/nginx/html/index.html
systemctl enable --now nginx
```

User data is convenient but slow when it does a lot (installing many packages on every new instance). For fast scale-out, bake the software into your own AMI and keep user data short.

### Key pairs

A **key pair** is a public/private key set used for SSH to Linux instances (and to decrypt the initial Administrator password on Windows). AWS stores the public key and places it on the instance; you download the private key (the .pem file) exactly once at creation. If you lose it, AWS cannot recover it. Treat the private key as a credential, and note that modern practice often replaces SSH keys entirely with AWS Systems Manager Session Manager. How to manage permissions and shared responsibility around this belongs to the cloud security lessons.

sections.heading: Pricing models: choosing how to pay for compute
sections.content:
The same instance can cost very different amounts depending on how you commit to it. The art is matching the payment model to how predictable the workload is.

| Model | How it works | Typical saving vs On-Demand | Best fit | Main risk |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| On-Demand | Pay per second (Linux) or per hour, no commitment | None (baseline) | Unpredictable, short-lived, first deployments | Highest unit price |
| Reserved Instances (RI) | Commit to a specific instance family/Region for 1 or 3 years | Up to about 72% | Steady, predictable workloads such as a database | Locked to a configuration; unused commitment is wasted |
| Savings Plans | Commit to dollars per hour of usage for 1 or 3 years | Up to about 66% (Compute) to 72% (EC2 Instance) | Steady baseline with flexibility to change size, family or Region | Overcommitting beyond your real baseline |
| Spot Instances | Bid on spare capacity at a variable price | Up to about 90% | Fault-tolerant, interruptible jobs: batch, CI, big data, stateless workers | AWS can reclaim the instance with a 2-minute warning |
| Dedicated Hosts / Instances | Physical server (or hardware) used by you alone | Priced at a premium | Per-socket software licenses, compliance rules requiring isolation | Highest cost, you manage host capacity |
| Capacity Reservations | Reserve capacity in one AZ, billed whether used or not | None by itself | Guaranteeing capacity for an event | Paying for idle capacity |

### Reading the table like a practitioner

**Reserved Instances versus Savings Plans.** Both trade commitment for discount. Savings Plans are the modern default because they follow your spend rather than a fixed instance configuration. A **Compute Savings Plan** also covers Fargate and Lambda and lets you move between Regions and families, while an **EC2 Instance Savings Plan** gives a deeper discount in exchange for fixing the family and Region. Convertible RIs allow exchanging configurations but with lower discounts.

**Spot** is the biggest saving and the biggest trap. A Spot instance can be interrupted at any time with a two-minute notice delivered through instance metadata and EventBridge. It is perfect for a worker pool that pulls jobs from a queue, and terrible for a single database or a stateful web server. Design for interruption: checkpoint work, keep workers stateless, and diversify across several instance types and AZs to reduce the chance of simultaneous reclaim.

**Dedicated Hosts** matter mainly for bring-your-own-license software tied to physical cores or sockets, not for general performance.

### The layered strategy

A mature design layers these: cover the always-on baseline with Savings Plans, handle normal variation with On-Demand through Auto Scaling, and push interruptible background work to Spot. The questions to ask: How predictable is the baseline over the next year? Can the work be restarted? Is there a licensing or isolation requirement? Cost Explorer and the Savings Plans recommendations use your actual usage to suggest the right commitment, which beats guessing.

sections.heading: Storage for compute: EBS, snapshots, instance store and EFS
sections.content:
An instance needs somewhere to keep data. AWS offers three very different answers, and choosing wrongly is a leading cause of data loss for newcomers.

### Amazon EBS: the network-attached disk

**Elastic Block Store (EBS)** provides block volumes that behave like a hard drive plugged into the instance, but they live on the network, separate from the host. Key properties: a volume exists in **one Availability Zone** and can attach only to instances in that same AZ; it persists independently of the instance when you stop it; and it is replicated within its AZ for durability. Most volumes attach to one instance at a time (io1 and io2 support Multi-Attach for special clustered cases).

| Volume type | Medium | Performance | Use case |
|---|---|---|---|
| gp3 (General Purpose SSD) | SSD | 3,000 IOPS and 125 MiB/s baseline, scalable to 16,000 IOPS and 1,000 MiB/s, independent of size | Default for boot volumes, web and app servers, small databases |
| gp2 (older General Purpose) | SSD | IOPS tied to volume size, with burst credits | Legacy; gp3 is usually cheaper and more predictable |
| io2 / io2 Block Express | SSD | Provisioned, up to 64,000 IOPS (256,000 on Block Express), highest durability | Latency-sensitive databases such as large Oracle or SQL Server |
| st1 (Throughput Optimized) | HDD | High sequential throughput | Big data, logs, streaming reads |
| sc1 (Cold HDD) | HDD | Lowest cost per GB | Infrequently accessed data |

A useful rule: start with **gp3**, move to **io2** only when you can prove you need sustained high IOPS, and remember that only SSD types can be boot volumes.

### Snapshots

An **EBS snapshot** is a point-in-time backup stored in S3 (managed by AWS, not visible as a bucket in your account). Snapshots are **incremental**: after the first full copy, only changed blocks are saved. Because they are regional, a snapshot is how you move data **between AZs** (create a snapshot, then a new volume from it in another AZ) and between Regions (copy the snapshot). Automate them with Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager or AWS Backup rather than relying on memory.

### Instance store: fast but ephemeral

Some instance types (i4i, d3, c6id) include **instance store** disks physically attached to the host. They are very fast and included in the price, but the data is lost when the instance is stopped, terminated, or the underlying hardware fails. It survives a simple reboot. Use it for caches, buffers and scratch data, never for the only copy of anything important.

### EFS in brief

**Elastic File System (EFS)** is a managed NFS file system for Linux. Unlike EBS it spans multiple AZs and can be mounted by hundreds of instances at once, growing and shrinking automatically; you pay for what you store. It suits shared content such as web assets or home directories.

The question to ask of any data: Can I afford to lose it if this instance disappears? If not, it belongs on EBS with snapshots, in EFS, or in a managed database or S3, not on instance store.

sections.heading: Elastic Load Balancing: ALB, NLB and GWLB
sections.content:
A **load balancer** is a single front door that spreads incoming requests across a group of servers and stops sending traffic to servers that are unhealthy. The analogy is a restaurant host who seats guests at open tables and skips sections that are closed. **Elastic Load Balancing (ELB)** is the managed family of load balancers; AWS runs and scales them across multiple AZs for you, and you reach them through a DNS name rather than a fixed IP.

### The three modern types

| Type | OSI layer | Protocols | Key strengths | Typical use |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Application Load Balancer (ALB) | 7 (application) | HTTP, HTTPS, gRPC, WebSocket | Routes by host name, URL path, header or query string; can target instances, IPs, Lambda functions | Websites, microservices, APIs |
| Network Load Balancer (NLB) | 4 (transport) | TCP, UDP, TLS | Millions of requests per second, very low latency, static IP per AZ, supports Elastic IPs | Gaming, IoT, non-HTTP protocols, fixed-IP needs |
| Gateway Load Balancer (GWLB) | 3 (network) | IP packets over GENEVE (port 6081) | Transparently inserts third-party virtual appliances such as firewalls into the traffic path | Inspection fleets |

The older **Classic Load Balancer** still exists for legacy applications, but new designs choose one of the three above. A good default: ALB for web traffic, NLB when you need raw TCP/UDP speed or static addresses, GWLB only when you operate network appliances.

### Listeners, rules and target groups

Three vocabulary words matter:

- A **listener** checks for connection requests on a protocol and port, for example HTTPS on 443. An HTTP listener on 80 commonly just redirects to HTTPS.
- A **rule** (ALB) decides what to do with a request, such as forward /api/* to one group and everything else to another.
- A **target group** is the pool of destinations (EC2 instances, IP addresses, or Lambda) that receive the forwarded traffic.

```text
Client -> ALB (listener :443)
            rule: path /api/*  -> target group api-tg  (3 instances)
            default            -> target group web-tg  (4 instances)
```

### Health checks

Each target group runs **health checks**: the load balancer requests a path such as /health on a port at an interval (for example every 30 seconds) and counts consecutive successes or failures against a **healthy threshold** and **unhealthy threshold**. A target that fails is taken out of rotation until it recovers. Two practical points: a health endpoint should check the application genuinely works (not merely that the port is open), and when you deregister or scale in a target, **deregistration delay** (default 300 seconds) lets in-flight requests finish.

### Cross-zone behavior

Load balancer nodes live in each enabled AZ. With **cross-zone load balancing**, every node spreads requests across targets in all AZs; it is on by default for ALB and off by default for NLB. If your targets are uneven across AZs and you leave it off, one AZ can get overloaded.

sections.heading: EC2 Auto Scaling: elasticity and self-healing
sections.content:
**Elasticity** means capacity follows demand automatically: more servers during a sale, fewer at 3 a.m. **EC2 Auto Scaling** delivers it by managing a group of instances called an **Auto Scaling group (ASG)**. The service itself costs nothing; you pay only for the instances and resources it launches.

### Launch templates

An ASG needs a recipe for new instances. A **launch template** stores that recipe: the AMI ID, instance type, key pair, security groups, storage, IAM instance profile and user data. Templates are **versioned**, so you can publish version 2 with a new AMI and roll it out with an **instance refresh**. (The older launch configurations are legacy and no longer recommended.) A template can also define a **mixed instances policy** that blends On-Demand and Spot across several instance types.

### Minimum, desired, maximum

Three numbers define the group's boundaries:

| Setting | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Minimum | Never fewer than this; your floor for availability | 2 |
| Desired | The number the group tries to run right now | 4 |
| Maximum | Never more than this; your cost ceiling | 10 |

Scaling policies change the **desired** value within the min and max bounds. The maximum is a safety valve: without a sensible cap, a runaway loop or an attack could scale you into a very large bill.

### Scaling policies

| Policy | How it decides | Good for |
|---|---|---|
| Target tracking | You pick a metric and a target value; the service adds or removes capacity to hold it, like a thermostat | Most workloads. Example: keep average CPU at 50 percent, or ALBRequestCountPerTarget at 1000 |
| Step scaling | CloudWatch alarm triggers different adjustments depending on how far the metric breached | Fine control, such as add 1 instance at 60 percent CPU but add 4 at 85 percent |
| Simple scaling | One alarm, one adjustment, then a cooldown wait | Legacy; step is usually better |
| Scheduled scaling | Changes capacity at set times | Known patterns: scale up at 08:45 before office hours |
| Predictive scaling | Uses machine learning on past load to scale ahead of recurring peaks | Cyclical traffic |

Target tracking is the right first choice. Pair it with an **instance warmup** time so new instances are not counted in metrics before they finish booting; otherwise the group overreacts.

### Self-healing

An ASG continuously checks instance health. By default it uses EC2 status checks only, so a crashed application on a running instance goes unnoticed. When the group is attached to a load balancer, **turn on ELB health checks** so an instance that fails the application-level check is terminated and replaced. Set a **health check grace period** long enough for boot and user data to finish, or healthy-but-starting instances will be killed in a loop.

### Pitfalls

Setting min equal to max disables elasticity (useful only for self-healing of a fixed fleet). Scaling on the wrong metric, such as CPU for an I/O-bound app, produces a group that never scales when it should. And an ASG with a single instance in one AZ heals itself but suffers downtime during every replacement.

sections.heading: Regions, Availability Zones and spreading across AZs
sections.content:
Where you place compute determines how it fails. AWS organizes its infrastructure in two layers.

A **Region** is a geographic area such as us-east-1 (N. Virginia) or eu-west-1 (Ireland). Regions are fully independent: separate pricing, separate service availability, and no automatic data replication between them. You choose a Region by latency to users, legal requirements on where data may reside, available services, and price.

An **Availability Zone (AZ)** is one or more discrete data centers inside a Region, with independent power, cooling and networking, connected to the other AZs by high-speed, low-latency links. Most Regions have three or more AZs, named like us-east-1a. The letter is mapped differently per AWS account to spread load, so for cross-account coordination use the **AZ ID** (for example use1-az1), which is the same for everyone.

### Why spreading matters

A single AZ is a single failure domain. A power event, network fault or capacity shortage in that AZ takes down everything placed only there. EBS volumes, subnets and instances each live in exactly one AZ, so high availability is something you build by **using more than one AZ**, not something you get automatically from running in a Region.

To make an ASG multi-AZ, you give it subnets in different AZs (the subnet design itself is covered in the separate VPC lesson). The group then:

1. Launches instances so that they are balanced as evenly as possible across the chosen AZs.
2. If an AZ becomes unhealthy or runs out of capacity, launches replacements in the remaining AZs.
3. **Rebalances** when the AZ recovers, sometimes launching a new instance before terminating an old one so capacity never dips.

```text
ASG: min 2, desired 4, max 8, subnets in 3 AZs
  us-east-1a: 2 instances
  us-east-1b: 1 instance
  us-east-1c: 1 instance
```

### Capacity math

Spreading has a cost-planning side effect. If you run two AZs and need 4 instances of capacity to carry peak load even after losing one AZ, you need 4 in each AZ, which is 8 in total, so half your fleet is idle most of the day. With three AZs, you need only 2 in each AZ (6 total) to survive losing one. More AZs means less over-provisioning per AZ for the same tolerance. The question to ask: if one AZ vanished right now, would the remaining instances carry the load while the group scales up?

### Pitfalls

Putting the ASG across AZs but the database in one AZ merely moves the single point of failure. Data transfer between AZs also carries a small per-GB charge, so chatty cross-AZ architectures cost more. And disk volumes cannot follow an instance to a new AZ, which is why stateless instances plus managed, replicated data stores are the standard pattern.

sections.heading: Other compute options at a glance
sections.content:
EC2 gives maximum control, but control means you patch, size and scale the servers. AWS offers a ladder of alternatives that trade control for convenience. Pick the highest rung that meets the requirements.

### Amazon Lightsail

**Lightsail** is the simplified entry point: a virtual private server with a predictable monthly price, bundling an instance, SSD storage, a static IP and a data transfer allowance. It offers one-click blueprints for WordPress, LAMP stacks, Node.js and others, plus simple load balancers, managed databases and snapshots. It is aimed at small websites, blogs, dev environments and learners who do not want to think about instance families, EBS types or subnet design. Its limits are the reason it is not used for large systems: far fewer instance sizes, simpler networking, and no deep integration with features such as Auto Scaling groups. Lightsail resources can connect to other AWS services when you outgrow it.

### The wider ladder

| Option | What you manage | Good for |
|---|---|---|
| EC2 | OS, runtime, scaling, patching | Full control, lift-and-shift, specialized software |
| AWS Elastic Beanstalk | Just your code; it provisions EC2, ELB and ASG for you | Developers who want a managed web app platform |
| Containers (ECS, EKS, Fargate) | Container images; Fargate removes the servers entirely | Microservices, portable packaging |
| AWS Lambda (serverless) | Only function code, billed per request and duration | Event-driven tasks, APIs with spiky traffic |
| AWS Batch | Job definitions; it runs them on EC2 or Spot | Large queues of batch jobs |
| AWS Outposts | AWS hardware racks installed in your own data center | Workloads that must stay on premises with local latency |

Containers and serverless have their own concepts (images, clusters, task definitions, cold starts, concurrency, event sources), and they are covered in a separate lesson. This lesson stays with servers you can log in to.

### Choosing

The questions to ask: Does the software need a specific operating system or kernel setting? Must it run constantly or only in response to events? How much operations effort can the team afford? A static brochure site may be best on Lightsail or S3. A traditional licensed application that runs 24/7 probably wants EC2 with a Savings Plan. An image-resize routine triggered by uploads is a natural Lambda function. Starting on EC2 is not wrong, but staying there out of habit when a managed option fits is a common source of avoidable operations work.

sections.heading: Worked example: a resilient web tier
sections.content:
Requirement: a customer website that stays up if a data center fails, absorbs a traffic spike on sale days, and does not pay for idle servers at night. We assemble the pieces from this lesson.

### The design

```text
                    Internet users
                          |
                  Route 53 (DNS name)
                          |
        Application Load Balancer (listener 443)
            /                           \
   subnet in us-east-1a          subnet in us-east-1b
   EC2 instances (web)           EC2 instances (web)
            \                           /
              Auto Scaling group
          min 2 / desired 2 / max 8
                          |
         Shared state kept OFF the instances
         (managed database Multi-AZ, S3 for uploads)
```

### Each piece and why it is there

| Component | Role | Why this choice |
|---|---|---|
| ALB with HTTPS listener | Single entry point, spreads requests, redirects HTTP to HTTPS | HTTP traffic needs layer 7 features and a stable DNS name |
| Target group web-tg | Pool of instances that receive traffic | Health check on /health every 30 seconds, 2 successes to be healthy, 3 failures to be removed |
| Launch template v1 | Recipe: golden AMI, m6i.large (or a Graviton m7g.large), security group, short user data | Pre-baked AMI keeps boot fast so scale-out is quick |
| Auto Scaling group across two AZs | Keeps the fleet at the right size and replaces failures | Min 2 with one instance per AZ means the loss of an AZ leaves a working server |
| Target tracking policy | Adds or removes instances to hold average CPU near 50 percent or request count per target steady | Elastic cost: low overnight, higher during the sale |
| ELB health checks turned on in the ASG | Replaces an instance whose application hangs | EC2 status checks alone would miss it |
| Data kept outside instances | Database with Multi-AZ, uploads in S3, sessions in a cache | Instances become disposable, so scaling in is safe |

### Walking through failures

1. **One instance's application crashes.** The ALB health check fails three times, traffic stops going to it, the ASG terminates and replaces it. Users never see an error beyond in-flight requests.
2. **The whole AZ us-east-1a goes dark.** The ALB routes everything to us-east-1b. The ASG sees the lost capacity and launches replacements in us-east-1b. For a few minutes the remaining instance carries the load, which is why min 2 is the floor and why you may choose min 4 for a busy site.
3. **Sale day.** Request count per target climbs, target tracking raises desired from 2 toward 8, and instances join the target group after the warmup period.

### Cost shaping

Cover the minimum fleet with a Savings Plan, let the burst instances run On-Demand, and optionally add a Spot share via a mixed instances policy since the instances are stateless. Set a CloudWatch billing alarm so a misbehaving policy is noticed early.

### Pitfalls to check in review

Is there any step that depends on one AZ (a single database, a single NAT, an EBS volume holding sessions)? Is the max value a deliberate cap? Does the health check endpoint reflect real application health? Is the launch template versioned and the AMI patched on a schedule? Network details such as subnets and security group rules belong to the VPC lesson, and access controls to the cloud security lessons.

quiz.question: A team stops a production EC2 instance overnight to save money. The instance uses a gp3 root volume and an auto-assigned public IP. What is true the next morning after they start it again?

options.label: The volume kept its data and was billed while stopped, but the auto-assigned public IPv4 address is different
The volume was deleted at stop, so the team must restore the server from an AMI before starting it again
No charges applied for any resource while stopped, and the public IP address stayed exactly the same
Only data on the instance store survived, while the gp3 root volume reverted to the original AMI contents

quiz.explanation: Stopping an EBS-backed instance stops compute billing but keeps the EBS volumes, which continue to be billed, and their data persists. An auto-assigned public IPv4 address is released at stop, so a new one is assigned on start unless an Elastic IP is used. The idea that the root volume is deleted describes termination, not stop. Claiming that nothing is billed ignores the EBS storage charge and the IP change. Instance store data is actually the data that does not survive a stop, and an EBS root volume does not revert to the AMI.

quiz.question: A company runs a nightly video transcoding job that reads tasks from a queue, can restart any task safely, and must cost as little as possible. Which purchasing option fits best?

options.label: Spot Instances, because the work is interruptible and restartable so the large discount outweighs the reclaim risk
A three-year Reserved Instance, because the nightly job is predictable and a commitment always gives the lowest price
A Dedicated Host, because dedicated hardware guarantees that the nightly job will never be interrupted by AWS
On-Demand Instances, because only On-Demand pricing can be combined with an Auto Scaling group for batch work

quiz.explanation: Spot offers savings of up to about 90 percent, and it suits stateless, fault-tolerant, restartable work such as queue-driven batch processing; a two-minute interruption notice is acceptable when tasks can be retried. A three-year Reserved Instance pays for capacity around the clock when the job runs only at night, so it wastes money. A Dedicated Host is a premium isolation and licensing option, not a cost saver. Auto Scaling groups can use Spot, On-Demand or a mix, so the claim that only On-Demand works is false.

quiz.question: An application serves HTTPS traffic and must send requests for /images/* to one set of servers and all other paths to another set. Which load balancer type should be used?

options.label: Network Load Balancer, since it supports TLS and gives the fastest layer 4 performance for any web traffic
Gateway Load Balancer, since it transparently distributes web requests across a fleet of virtual appliances
Application Load Balancer, since it works at layer 7 and can route by URL path using listener rules and target groups
Classic Load Balancer, since it is the only type that can forward traffic to more than one pool of servers

quiz.explanation: Path-based routing needs inspection of the HTTP request, which is a layer 7 function provided by the Application Load Balancer through listener rules that forward to different target groups. The Network Load Balancer operates at layer 4 and does not look at URL paths, even though it can terminate TLS. The Gateway Load Balancer is for inserting third-party network appliances into the traffic path. The Classic Load Balancer is legacy and lacks path-based rules, and it is not the only option for multiple pools.

quiz.question: An Auto Scaling group has min 2, desired 4, max 10 and is attached to an ALB. The application on one instance hangs, but the instance still passes EC2 status checks and is never replaced. What is the most likely fix?

options.label: Raise the maximum capacity to 20 so the group has more room to launch new instances automatically
Switch the volumes from gp3 to io2 so the application can no longer hang because of disk latency
Replace the target tracking policy with a scheduled action that restarts every instance at midnight
Enable ELB health checks on the group so a target failing the load balancer check is terminated and replaced

quiz.explanation: By default an Auto Scaling group relies only on EC2 status checks, which verify the virtual machine, not the application. Turning on ELB health checks makes the group act on the load balancer verdict and replace the failing instance, with a grace period to cover boot time. Raising the maximum changes scaling headroom but not health detection. Changing the volume type is a guess about disk latency unrelated to the symptom. A midnight restart is a blunt workaround that leaves the daytime failure undetected.

quiz.question: A web tier runs in an Auto Scaling group where every instance sits in one Availability Zone. Leadership asks for resilience to the loss of a data center. What is the correct change?

options.label: Choose a larger instance family so that a single stronger server can survive hardware faults on its own
Give the group subnets in at least two Availability Zones, so it balances instances across them and replaces lost capacity
Increase the desired capacity inside the same zone, since many instances in one zone are independent failure domains
Copy the AMI to another Region and rely on EBS to move the running volumes automatically between zones

quiz.explanation: An Availability Zone is the failure domain for power, cooling and networking, so resilience comes from spreading across at least two of them. An Auto Scaling group with subnets in several zones balances instances and launches replacements in the surviving zones. A bigger instance is still in the same zone and fails with it. More instances in one zone share the same failure domain. Copying an AMI to another Region is a disaster-recovery step and does not make running EBS volumes move; volumes are bound to a single zone.
